fields.h1: How to Honor God with Your Money
fields.meta_title: How to Honor God with Your Money
fields.description: What we do with money reveals what we love. Here is how to honor God with it — as stewards, giving generously, guarding against greed, and storing treasure in heaven.
fields.body_html:
Jesus talked about money more than almost any other subject, and for good reason: what we do with our money reveals what we truly believe and love. Money is not evil — it is a good gift and a useful servant — but it is a dangerous master, and the human heart is prone to trust it, love it, and serve it in the place of God. Learning to handle money in a way that honours God is therefore not a minor matter of budgeting but a central part of discipleship — a daily test of whether we trust and love God more than we trust and love what money can buy. “For where your treasure is, there your heart will be also” (Matthew 6:21). Get money right, and a great many other things fall into place; get it wrong, and it quietly corrupts everything. Here is how to honour God with what he has entrusted to you.

Remember it all belongs to God

The foundation of a godly view of money is a single truth: it is not ultimately ours. We are stewards, not owners — managers entrusted with resources that belong to God, and answerable to him for how we use them. “The earth is the Lord’s and the fullness thereof” (Psalm 24:1), and everything we have, including our ability to earn, comes from his hand. This changes everything. If our money is really God’s, then the question is no longer “How much of my money should I give to God?” but “How does God want me to use his money?”

This stewardship mindset frees us from both greed and anxiety. We can hold our possessions loosely, because they were never truly ours to clutch, and we can trust the Owner to provide, because he has promised to. Jesus warned that we cannot serve two masters: “You cannot serve God and money” (Matthew 6:24). One of them will rule. The steward who remembers whose money it is keeps money in its proper place — a tool for serving God, never a rival to him.

Give generously and cheerfully

A heart that honours God with money is, above all, a generous heart. Giving is woven all through Scripture — supporting the work of God, caring for the poor, and sharing with those in need. And God loves not grudging duty but glad generosity: “Each one must give as he has decided in his heart, not reluctantly or under compulsion, for God loves a cheerful giver” (2 Corinthians 9:7). Generosity is meant to be a joy, not a burden — the overflow of a heart grateful for all it has received.

There is even a beautiful paradox in it: giving enriches the giver. “Whoever sows sparingly will also reap sparingly, and whoever sows bountifully will also reap bountifully” (2 Corinthians 9:6), and Jesus himself said, “It is more blessed to give than to receive” (Acts 20:35). Those who have learned to give discover a freedom and joy that the tight-fisted never know. So make giving a settled, planned, glad habit — honouring God with the firstfruits, not the leftovers: “Honor the Lord with your wealth and with the firstfruits of all your produce” (Proverbs 3:9).

Guard your heart against the love of money

Scripture is realistic about money’s spiritual danger. The problem is not money itself but our love of it: “For the love of money is a root of all kinds of evils. It is through this craving that some have wandered away from the faith and pierced themselves with many pangs” (1 Timothy 6:10). The love of money is subtle; it can grip the poor and the rich alike, showing itself in greed, anxiety, envy, and a life organized around getting and keeping.

The remedy is contentment and trust. Paul pairs the warning with a promise: “Keep your life free from love of money, and be content with what you have, for he has said, ‘I will never leave you nor forsake you’” (Hebrews 13:5). When God himself is our security, we no longer need money to be. Some of the most God-honouring believers in history proved this in extreme ways — trusting God for their daily needs and giving away fortunes — and found him faithful. Their lives are a standing rebuke to the anxious grasping of our age and a witness that God can be trusted to provide.

Be faithful and honest in the small things

Honouring God with money is not only about giving; it is about integrity in earning, spending, and managing. God cares how we handle every part of it — that we work honestly, pay what we owe, keep our word, and manage wisely rather than wastefully. Jesus taught that faithfulness in money is a test of character: “One who is faithful in a very little is also faithful in much... If then you have not been faithful in the unrighteous wealth, who will entrust to you the true riches?” (Luke 16:10–11).

This dignifies the ordinary work of budgeting, saving, and diligent labour. Avoiding debt where we can, living within our means, providing for our families, planning wisely — these are not unspiritual concerns but part of faithful stewardship. The believer who is careless, dishonest, or reckless with money dishonours God, however much they may give; the one who is diligent and honest in the small things honours him in the whole. Faithfulness in money is training for faithfulness in everything.

Trust God to provide

Much of our anxious and grasping relationship with money is rooted in a quiet fear that we will not have enough. Jesus met that fear head-on. He pointed to the birds, who neither sow nor reap yet are fed, and the flowers, clothed more gloriously than Solomon, and said, “Therefore do not be anxious, saying, ‘What shall we eat?’... For your heavenly Father knows that you need them all” (Matthew 6:31–32). The cure for money-anxiety is not a bigger balance but a bigger trust in a Father who has promised to provide.

This trust is what makes radical generosity possible. If God is truly our provider, we can give freely, knowing the supply does not finally depend on our hoarding. Paul assures the generous Philippians, “And my God will supply every need of yours according to his riches in glory in Christ Jesus” (Philippians 4:19). Countless believers have proved this promise, giving beyond what seemed prudent and finding God faithful to meet their needs. When we seek first his kingdom, he takes responsibility for the rest — and a heart resting in his provision is finally free from money’s grip.

Store up treasure in heaven

Jesus lifted the whole subject of money onto an eternal horizon. “Do not lay up for yourselves treasures on earth, where moth and rust destroy and where thieves break in and steal, but lay up for yourselves treasures in heaven... For where your treasure is, there your heart will be also” (Matthew 6:19–21). Earthly wealth is temporary and cannot be taken beyond the grave; but money invested in God’s kingdom — in generosity, in the gospel, in the good of others — becomes treasure that lasts forever.

Paul urged the rich to make exactly this exchange: “to do good, to be rich in good works, to be generous and ready to share, thus storing up treasure for themselves as a good foundation for the future” (1 Timothy 6:18–19). This is the wisest possible use of money — to convert what cannot last into what cannot perish. Every act of generosity is a deposit in a bank that no thief can reach and no crash can ruin.

Where to begin

So how do you start honouring God with your money? Begin by settling the foundation: acknowledge that it all belongs to God and ask him to make you a faithful steward. Make giving a planned, glad, first priority rather than an afterthought. Guard your heart against greed by cultivating contentment and trust. Be scrupulously honest and diligent in earning, spending, and managing. And lift your eyes to eternity, investing in what will outlast this world.

Above all, remember that this is finally a matter of the heart, not merely the wallet. Jesus does not want your money so much as he wants you — and how you handle money is one of the truest signs of whether he has your heart. Trust the God who feeds the birds and clothes the fields to provide for you, hold your possessions with an open hand, and use his gifts to bless others and advance his kingdom. A life that honours God with money is a life set free from one of the strongest chains there is — and rich toward God, which is the only wealth that lasts. Start where you are, with what you have; God is not waiting for you to be wealthy, but for you to be faithful, and the smallest gift offered in love and trust is precious in his sight.
